The macrophages appear as reddish cells in the aqueous and the trabecular meshwork has a reddish-brown discoloration. Ghost-cell glaucoma occurs in association with vitreous hemorrhage. The degenerated RBCs appear as tan-colored spheres known as ghost cells, which contain clumps of denatured hemoglobin. question: 3 yr old boy Patient refered from peadiatric after he was diagnosed with Usher syndrome based on hearing loss and vestibular finding . On examination you found XT 35 PD .. what is the most appropriate next diagnostics step ?
explanation: ERG is better The XT that he has is most likely sensory. It depends on the type of Usher syndrome. It could be Cogan syndrome also. - Cogan syndrome: rare systemic autoimmune vasculitis characterized by intraocular inflammation and vestibuloauditory dysfunction (particularly neurosensory) developing within months of each other. The disease primarily occurs in young adults, with both sexes affected equally; children can also be affected. Investigations: ESR and CRP elevated WBC, Antibodies to inner ear antigens may be detectable, MRI may show inner ear and other abnormalities. - Usher syndrome: the most common name used to describe the association of RP with congenital sensorineural hearing loss, whether partial or profound. There are 3 types of Usher syndrome, with types 1 and 2 being more common than type 3. Type 1 have early and profound deafness, RP, extinguished ERG, and vestibular areflexia. Patients with type 2 are born with moderate to severe hearing loss and develop RP within the second decade of life but have normal vestibular function. Patients with type 3 have progressive hearing loss, RP of variable severity, and sporadic vestibular function.

question: lower lid lesion excision (pic, less than 1 third of lid), how to repair?
explanation: Since the defect is <33%, the answer is primary closure. - Direct closure is used for defects less than 33% of the lid width. - For defects that involve 33-50% of the lid width, the eyelid can be freed with a lateral canthotomy and then a semicircular flap (a.k.a. Tenzel flap) is rotated into the defect. - The Cutler-Beard procedure is used when the upper eyelid defect is greater than 50% of the eyelid width. - Greater than 50% defects of the lower eyelid are repaired with a modified Hughes procedure.

question: Mechanism of TAO:
explanation: the presumed mechanism is activation of orbital fibroblasts by Graves' disease-related autoantibodies, which lead to the release of T cell chemoattractants, initiating an interaction which ultimately results in fibroblasts expressing extracellular matrix molecules, biologic materials proliferating and differentiating into myofibroblasts or lipofibroblasts and deposition of glycosaminoglycans which bind water that lead to swelling, congestion in addition to connective tissue remodeling. This results in extraocular muscle enlargement and orbital fat expansion. Reference: https://eyewiki.org/Thyroid_Eye_Disease Orbital vs preseptal what's the difference:

options.B: b blockers ( they didn't mention topical or oral)

explanation: also Beta-blockers if they are topical This a case of Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis/Posner-Schlossman Syndrome, treatment includes: - Topical β-blocker (e.g., timolol 0.5% daily or b.i.d.), topical α-2 agonist (e.g., brimonidine 0.1% to 0.2% b.i.d. to t.i.d.), topical CAI (e.g., dorzolamide 2% b.i.d. to t.i.d.). - Short course (1 week) of topical steroids (e.g., prednisolone acetate 1% q.i.d.) - Oral indomethacin (e.g., 75 to 150 mg p.o. daily) or topical NSAIDs (e.g., ketorolac q.i.d.). - Consider a systemic CAI (e.g., acetazolamide 500 mg sequel p.o. b.i.d.) if IOP is significantly increased and unresponsive to topical therapy (rare). - Hyperosmotic agents (e.g., mannitol 20% 1 to 2 g/kg i.v. over 45 minutes) or anterior chamber paracentesis can be considered when the IOP is determined to be dangerously high for the involved optic nerve. - Consider a cycloplegic agent (e.g., cyclopentolate 1% t.i.d.) if the patient is symptomatic. Reference: The Wills Eye Manual (Page 418)

question: Unformed hallucinations with congruence VF defect the lesion is in:
explanation: Hallucinations are defined as perceptions that occur in the absence of a corresponding external sensory stimulus. Visual hallucinations can be classified as unformed/simple (e.g., dots, flashes, zig-zags) or formed/complex (actual objects or people). Occipital lobe lesions will show unformed hallucinations while temporal lobe lesions will show formed hallucinations.

explanation: Perioperative posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is a rare but devastating condition. Visual impairment is commonly bilateral, profound, and irreversible. The most frequently associated triggering events are spine surgeries, other orthopedic surgeries, cardiac bypass surgeries, and radical neck dissection.
